annotation_description: Discarding Meticulous Archive (a tapped dual land with surveil) over Swamp when the deck likely wants UB for Psychic Frog on turn 2 and the Archive provides both W and U. However, the player has Flooded Strand and Marsh Flats which can fetch similar lands, and keeping Swamp ensures black mana access through Marsh Flats. The real question is whether Hedge Maze (tapped Forest/Island with surveil) should have been discarded instead, since the deck appears to be UBw and Forest mana is less relevant in the near term. Meticulous Archive at least provides Plains/Island types for fetch targets. That said, with Marsh Flats able to fetch Swamp or Plains, and Flooded Strand able to fetch Plains or Island, having a basic Swamp is somewhat redundant. Discarding the basic Swamp would preserve more flexibility in land types available. The choice is close but Swamp was arguably the better discard since fetchlands already cover black mana needs.

The player appears to be evoking Solitude (exiling the other Solitude as the white card pitch cost) while the opponent has no creatures on the battlefield, wasting two copies of Solitude for no value. Solitude's ETB exiles 'up to one other target creature' so it can enter with no target, but the evoke sacrifice means it dies immediately - netting nothing meaningful.

annotation_description: The player chose to hard-cast Solitude for 3WW when they only have 2 lands in play (based on the board state showing Turn 3 with Meticulous Archive and Marsh Flats in graveyard). They cannot pay 3WW with the mana available. Meanwhile, they could have evoked Solitude by exiling Atraxa, Grand Unifier (a white card) from hand. Atraxa is a 7-mana card that's very unlikely to be castable soon, and evoking Solitude would exile the opponent's threat immediately. By choosing to hard-cast, they're either making an illegal play or wasting the opportunity to remove a threat. The reasoning states 'no white cards to exile' but Atraxa, Grand Unifier is white (it costs 3GWUB and is a white card).

Evoking or casting Solitude when the opponent has zero creatures on the battlefield. Additionally, this is their own precombat main phase where they should be developing their board with Psychic Frog and playing a land.

The opponent has no creatures on the battlefield, so Solitude's ETB exile ability has no valid target to remove. Casting Solitude now (presumably by evoking it, exiling a white card) wastes both the Solitude and the exiled white card for no value - there's nothing to exile. Even if hard-casting, spending 5 mana on a 3/2 lifelink with no ETB value is poor when the opponent has no board. The player should be developing their mana base (they have Flooded Strand and Swamp in hand) and setting up for Atraxa or Superior Spider-Man instead.

message: You may choose an alternative cost
annotation_description: Player chose to hard-cast Solitude for {3}{W}{W} with only 2 lands in play, making this impossible to pay. Their reasoning that they had no white cards to exile for Evoke was incorrect — Atraxa, Grand Unifier is a white card. However, even Evoking Solitude here against an empty opponent board would be wasteful (sacrificing Atraxa and the Solitude for no exile value). The correct play was likely to not cast Solitude at all and instead develop the board with Flooded Strand + Psychic Frog.

Discarding Swamp over a duplicate Solitude is debatable. With only 2 lands on board (Godless Shrine and Hedge Maze) and expensive cards in hand (Atraxa at 7 mana, Superior Spider-Man at 4 mana), keeping land drops is important. The player has two copies of Solitude, and one can be used as Evoke fodder (exiling a white card) to cast the other for free. However, discarding a second Solitude still leaves one Solitude that can be hard-cast or evoked by exiling another white card. Meanwhile, Swamp provides a guaranteed land drop and black mana source for Psychic Frog or other spells. Flooded Strand already fetches Islands/Plains but not Swamps directly, so having Swamp in hand ensures black mana access.

Emperor of Bones is a 2-mana creature that could be relevant in this game, especially with creatures already in graveyards (Solitude in opponent's graveyard, Flickerwisp in own graveyard). It can exile cards from graveyards and reanimate them temporarily when it adapts. With the opponent playing a graveyard-interactive deck (Solitude already used), Emperor of Bones provides both a cheap threat and graveyard interaction. Discarding Overlord of the Balemurk or Ephemerate (which needs a creature in play to be useful) could be better choices. Overlord costs 5 mana (or impending for 2) but the player seems to be struggling with mana (no lands in play visible, suggesting something unusual about the game state). Ephemerate without creatures is dead. However, Emperor of Bones is castable for just 2 mana and provides a body plus utility, making it arguably worth keeping over cards like Ephemerate (no creatures to target) or Overlord (expensive).

When discarding to hand size, KimiK2 Vorthos discarded Psychic Frog instead of a more expendable card. Psychic Frog is a strong 2-drop that can grow, gain flying, and draw cards on combat damage. With only 2 lands in play and needing to develop the board, Psychic Frog would be one of the first cards they could actually cast. Meanwhile, Atraxa (7 mana) is extremely far from being castable with only 2 lands, and a second copy of Solitude could also be discarded since they already have one for evoke purposes. Discarding the cheap, efficient threat over an uncastable 7-drop is a meaningful value loss.

Evoked Solitude (exiling the other Solitude from hand as the white card) during opponent's combat with no enemy creatures on the battlefield. The 'up to one' targeting means no creature gets exiled, and the evoked Solitude is immediately sacrificed. This wastes two powerful cards for zero meaningful impact.

Discarding Watery Grave instead of a less useful card. With only 2 lands on the battlefield (Godless Shrine and Hedge Maze), KimiK2 Vorthos is severely mana-screwed and needs to hit land drops desperately. Watery Grave provides Island and Swamp mana types, which would help cast many of the powerful spells in hand (Psychic Frog at UB, Superior Spider-Man at 2UB, Force of Negation at 1UU). They also have Flooded Strand which can fetch a Plains or Island but not a Swamp - so Watery Grave provides unique Swamp access that Flooded Strand cannot fetch (though Godless Shrine already provides B). However, the real issue is that with only 2 lands in play and needing to get to 4+ mana, discarding any land is questionable. A second copy of Solitude (which can be evoked for free) or Atraxa (which costs 7 mana and is uncastable for many turns) would have been better discard choices.

During the end step, KimiK2 Vorthos chose to evoke Solitude (exiling a white card from hand) but has no targets on the opponent's battlefield to exile — GPT5n Spike has no creatures in play. Meanwhile, they could have used Psychic Frog's discard ability to pump it (discarding Atraxa to grow Frog and set up Goryo's Vengeance on Atraxa next turn), or cracked Flooded Strand to fix mana. Evoking Solitude with no meaningful target wastes a premium removal spell. More importantly, the reasoning text suggests confusion — they say 'pass and move to opponent's turn' but actually chose Solitude, suggesting a misclick or misunderstanding of what they were doing.

Discarding Goryo's Vengeance to pump Psychic Frog is wasteful. Goryo's Vengeance is a powerful instant that can reanimate Atraxa, Grand Unifier (a legendary creature in the graveyard) at instant speed, providing a massive 7/7 with flying, vigilance, deathtouch, lifelink and drawing multiple cards from its ETB trigger. The player has two copies and is discarding one for a mere +1/+1 counter on a Frog that is already tapped and done attacking this turn. While having a second copy mitigates this somewhat, throwing away such a high-impact card for incremental damage is a poor trade, especially when there are lower-value cards in hand (like Plains) that could be discarded instead if pumping was desired.

Casting Goryo's Vengeance during their own combat phase means Atraxa will be exiled at the beginning of their own end step this turn, getting only the ETB trigger. If cast during the opponent's end step instead, Atraxa would survive through their next turn, allowing a 7/7 flying lifelink deathtouch attack (gaining 7 life and dealing 7 damage) before being exiled at the beginning of that turn's end step.

Failed to crack Flooded Strand before Atraxa's ETB trigger resolves. Thinning a land from the library before revealing top 10 cards slightly improves the quality of Atraxa's reveal, increasing the chance of hitting more card types and better cards.

Declined to pump Psychic Frog by discarding a card before combat damage, missing an extra point of damage against an opponent with no blockers. With the opponent at 16 life and no blockers, discarding a low-value card like Plains to pump Psychic Frog from 1/2 to 2/3 would deal 1 extra damage (9 instead of 8) while still drawing a card from combat damage. Could also have cracked Flooded Strand for deck thinning.

message: Select a card of each card type (selected 0)
annotation_description: This is Atraxa's ETB trigger resolving, revealing 10 cards where you can select one card of each card type. The first card selected was Force of Negation (instant), which is fine as the instant pick. However, this appears to be just the first selection in a multi-step process. The revealed cards include Atraxa (creature), Shadowy Backstreet/Marsh Flats (land), Ephemerate (instant), March of Otherworldly Light (instant), Winternight Stories (sorcery), and Thoughtseize (sorcery). Force of Negation is a reasonable instant pick, but Ephemerate would arguably be stronger here - it enables re-triggering Atraxa for another 10-card reveal and has rebound for a second use. With Atraxa on the battlefield, Ephemerate generates enormous value and is likely the best instant to select from this reveal.

Discarded the second Psychic Frog to pump the attacking one instead of first playing Flooded Strand as a land drop and then discarding a less valuable card. The second Psychic Frog is a meaningful backup threat, especially with the opponent at 16 life and only one tapped land. They should have played Flooded Strand first (land drop), then discarded Flooded Strand or kept the second Frog for later deployment.

Discarding Quantum Riddler to pump Psychic Frog is reasonable for graveyard synergy, but discarding Flooded Strand instead would preserve more optionality. Quantum Riddler has a Warp cost of {1}{U} which could be cast more easily than the full 3UU, and with the opponent at 12 life and KimiK2 holding two Force of Negations for protection, keeping the Riddler as a potential threat while discarding the less impactful Flooded Strand (KimiK2 already has 6 lands including an untapped Flooded Strand on board) would be slightly better. However, the reanimation angle with Goryo's Vengeance in the graveyard doesn't work since Quantum Riddler isn't legendary, and the Warp ability does let you cast it from graveyard, so there's some merit to putting it there. This is close but slightly suboptimal.

Discarded Solitude, which is one of the most important cards in hand. With only 2 lands on turn 14, Solitude's evoke ability (exile a white card from hand) provides free removal and pairs with Ephemerate for a devastating combo: evoke Solitude to exile opponent's creature, then Ephemerate it to keep it on battlefield permanently and get a second exile trigger. This is the classic Modern Solitude + Ephemerate line.

Playing Hallowed Fountain before casting Thoughtseize is suboptimal sequencing. The player should cast Thoughtseize first (they already have black mana from Godless Shrine) to see the opponent's hand before committing to a land drop. Additionally, playing Flooded Strand instead of Hallowed Fountain would be better since the fetch land can be cracked later to enable Revolt for Fatal Push or to thin the deck, and avoids the 2-life payment decision. More importantly, with a 6/7 menace Psychic Frog and the opponent at 12 life with only 2 lands and no creatures, the priority should be casting Thoughtseize first to strip any potential answer (like a board wipe or removal spell) before combat, rather than playing a land that doesn't change available mana for the Thoughtseize.

The player is being Thoughtseized (opponent's spell on the stack forcing them to discard a nonland card). They chose to discard Force of Negation, but their reasoning says they're discarding it to Psychic Frog's ability to grow it. However, this is a Thoughtseize - the opponent is choosing what to discard. Wait - the message says 'Select a card (discard cost)' which suggests this is actually the player choosing what to discard. Looking more carefully: Thoughtseize is on the stack, but the player is KimiK2 Vorthos selecting a card. Thoughtseize says 'Target player reveals their hand. You choose a nonland card from it.' So GPT5n Spike cast Thoughtseize targeting KimiK2 Vorthos, but the system is asking KimiK2 Vorthos to select - this seems like the target is choosing, which shouldn't happen with Thoughtseize. Actually, looking at the 'After' text: 'KimiK2 Vorthos discards Force of Negation (source: Psychic Frog)' - so this is actually a Psychic Frog activation happening while Thoughtseize is on the stack. The player is discarding to Psychic Frog to pump it in response to Thoughtseize. This is actually reasonable - pumping the Frog before Thoughtseize resolves. But by discarding Force of Negation to the Frog, they're giving up a powerful free counterspell. The Flooded Strand would be the better discard to Psychic Frog since it's a land and provides less value from hand. However, Psychic Frog's ability says 'Discard a card' - it doesn't restrict to nonland. Discarding Flooded Strand would also give a +1/+1 counter while preserving Force of Negation. Thoughtseize will then resolve and the opponent will choose from the remaining cards - but keeping Force of Negation would be much more valuable than keeping Flooded Strand.

KimiK2 Vorthos resolved a Thoughtseize against GPT5n Spike and chose to discard Thoughtseize — a 1-mana sorcery that is far less threatening than the other options in the opponent's hand. The opponent has Teferi, Time Raveler (which shuts down instant-speed interaction and draws cards), Overlord of the Balemurk (a powerful 5/5 that mills and recurs creatures), Ephemerate (which can rebuy ETB effects repeatedly), and two Fatal Pushes that can kill Psychic Frog. Teferi is particularly devastating because it prevents KimiK2 from casting Force of Negation (their only card in hand besides a land) at instant speed, and its -3 can bounce Psychic Frog while drawing a card. Taking Thoughtseize over Teferi or Overlord of the Balemurk is a massive misplay.
Psychic Frog was already at sufficient power (6+) to deal lethal damage to the opponent at 6 life with no blockers. Discarding a card to pump it further wastes a card for pure overkill damage.
